description: We’re a crew of 5 builders from Cairo 🚀 We turn NASA data into tools people actually want to use, mixing web development, Python, 3D visualization and data crunching. We move fast, think big, and love a good challenge under pressure. Looking for one more explorer who’s curious about space, loves data, and wants to build something out of this world. Ready for launch?
summary: Refaey on the Moon is a web app for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. At the Moon's south pole, the Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so a single ridge can cut a lander's solar power and its direct radio link to Earth. Our app lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly: a guide character, Refaey, walks you through choosing a site, standing on it in 3D, seeing the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, comparing sites, and picking a launch date. Then it tells you what went wrong and what would have been better. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons, and the terrain horizon from NASA's LRO laser altimeter (LOLA). We checked the results against JPL Horizons and published NASA values. It turns a complicated expert task into a few clear choices, so anyone can understand why site and timing matter for power and communication at the lunar poles.
details:
Refaey on the Moon is a lunar landing-site navigator for the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, and a single ridge can decide whether a lander gets power or can see Earth. You pick a site and a landing date, and the app shows, through each lunar day, when the Sun clears the real terrain (power) and when Earth is in view (communications). It also shows how long until sunset and Earthset, and the best landing windows across several months.

How it works. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons. The horizon is the real skyline, traced in 720 directions from NASA LOLA elevation maps (PGDA products 81 and 90). The Sun counts as "up" when any part of its disk clears that skyline. We checked our engine carefully: its Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.01°, it matches the Sun angles at four Apollo landings within 0.1°, and over a full year at the IM-2 site it agrees with NASA's long-term illumination maps within 3 percentage points. Every number on screen carries a label saying where it came from.

The story. Refaey, our guide, is a fictional astronaut whose launch slipped. You become his mission planner. First he walks you through six real landings: Apollo 11, Apollo 15, Lunokhod 1, Chang'e 4, Chandrayaan-3 and Athena. Each one is placed on its site's real terrain at the minute of touchdown, with the Sun and Earth computed from JPL Horizons for that minute, and teaches one lesson about power, communications or timing. Then you plan his landing step by step. The conversations use choice buttons rather than AI chat, and any fact Refaey states comes with a "How do you know?" link to its source.

Impact. It gives mission planners a quick first look at a site, and gives teachers and students an honest feel for why south-pole landings are so hard.

Tools. React, TypeScript and Vite; Three.js (React Three Fiber) and GSAP for the 3D Moon and terrain; Node.js scripts for terrain processing and Python for the sprite pipeline; Vercel, with a serverless proxy for Horizons; Vitest and Playwright for tests.

Limits and next steps. Trip time from launch to landing is assumed (7.72 days, like IM-1). Dust, light scattered by terrain and ground stations on Earth are not modelled. At the Shackleton Rim point our Earth visibility still differs from NASA's long-term map, and we are checking the terrain data there. Next: let users choose the trip type, add more sites and a north-pole set.

What we considered. Scientific honesty: we label the limits of our data, such as the terrain resolution near each site. Accessibility: keyboard use, a reduced-motion setting and readable contrast. Performance on weak laptops and projectors. A source for every claim.
